summary: Defines the "body" extension for Sieve, the email filtering language. It adds a test that checks whether given strings appear in the body of a message, rather than only in headers. It is a standards-track specification.

eli5.summary: Email filters usually look at the envelope, like the sender. This adds a way to peek at the letter inside for certain words.

questions: how to filter email by message body in sieve
what is the sieve body test
how to match email body in sieve
sieve body raw vs text vs content
subtitle: How a Sieve mail filter can look inside the body of a message, not just its headers.

tldr.problem: The base Sieve language had no test for message bodies. A body test had been discussed early on but was removed as too costly to implement, even though several server vendors had built some form of it.
tldr.mechanism: This RFC adds a capability named "body" and a body test. A transform keyword (:raw, :content or :text) decides which parts of the body are matched against the key strings.
tldr.outcome: Filters can sort mail by body content, but the RFC warns that text matches are no replacement for a spam, virus or other security filtering system. It updates RFC 5229.

today: RFC 5173 is a Proposed Standard published in April 2008. It updates RFC 5229 and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Why a Body Test Is Needed
sections.content:
Sieve is an email filtering language. Its base document does not let a script look at what a message actually says, only at its headers. The body test checks for one or more strings in the body of an email message.

Such a test was discussed for the base Sieve document but removed because it was thought to be too costly to implement. The RFC notes that several server vendors implemented some form of it anyway, so this document brings the test back as an extension and pins down its syntax and meaning.

A script enables it by naming the capability string body in a require line.
sections.eli5: Mail filters could read the address on the envelope but not the letter. This extension lets them read the letter too, because many mail systems had already added it in their own ways.

sections.title: The body Test
sections.content:
The usage line is body [COMPARATOR] [MATCH-TYPE] [BODY-TRANSFORM] <key-list: string-list>. The test matches anything that follows the first empty line after the header. The empty line itself is not part of the body.

The comparator and match type come from the base Sieve document. The defaults are i;ascii-casemap and :is. The body transform decides which strings are pulled out of the body for matching.

If a message has only a header and no empty line after it, there is nothing to match, so every body test returns false, even one that looks for an empty string. This mirrors how the header test fails when the named header fields are absent.

The transforms do not match line by line, so the strings usually contain CRLFs. How those can be matched is governed by the comparator and match type: they can be written literally in a key, matched with the star and question-mark wildcards of :matches, or skipped with :contains.
sections.eli5: The test reads everything after the blank line that ends the message's top part. If the message has no letter at all, the answer is always no.

sections.title: Body Transforms: :raw and :text
sections.content:
A body transform is chosen with one of three keywords: :raw, :content with a list of content types, or :text. The default is :text.

:raw matches the entire undecoded body as a single item. MIME structure is irrelevant. The implementation MUST NOT remove any transfer encoding, MUST NOT refuse to filter messages with syntactic errors (unless its environment rejects them outright), and MUST treat multipart boundaries and the MIME headers of enclosed parts as ordinary content.

:text matches against an implementation's best effort at extracting UTF-8 text from the message. It is unspecified whether this yields one string or several, but all text from a given non-container MIME part MUST be in the same string. A simple implementation MAY treat :text as :content "text". A sophisticated one MAY strip mark-up, or convert other media types to text, for example by applying optical character recognition to images.

An example from the RFC: body :raw :contains "MAKE MONEY FAST" followed by discard; drops any message that contains that literal text in its body parts or in MIME headers other than the outermost header.
sections.eli5: :raw is like reading a letter with all the wrapping paper still on it. :text is like unwrapping it and reading just the words, doing your best to make sense of them.

sections.title: Matching MIME Parts with :content
sections.content:
With :content, the MIME parts whose content type is in the given list are searched one by one. A content type that begins or ends with a slash, or contains several slashes, matches nothing. One with a slash is a full type/subtype pair. One without a slash is a type only, and any subtype matches. The empty string matches all content types.

The search is recursive and descends into multipart and message/rfc822 parts. For a matching multipart part, only its prologue and epilogue are searched, each as a separate string. For a matching message/rfc822 part, only the header of the nested message is searched, as a single string. Other types are searched as one whole string. Matching against a container type with an empty string is a way to test that such a part exists.

Comparisons are performed on octets. Implementations decode the content transfer encoding and convert text to UTF-8 before comparing. They MUST support quoted-printable, base64, 7bit, 8bit and binary, and MUST be able to convert US-ASCII, ISO-8859-1 and the US-ASCII subset of ISO-8859-* to UTF-8. Parts that cannot be decoded MAY be treated as plain US-ASCII, omitted, or handled by local convention. A NUL octet SHOULD NOT end the comparison early.

Each part is matched independently, so a search expression MUST NOT match across MIME part boundaries, and the MIME headers of the containing part MUST NOT be included in the data.
sections.eli5: Mail can be a box with smaller boxes inside. :content lets you say which kinds of boxes to open, and each box is searched on its own, never mixing words from two boxes.

sections.title: Interaction with Other Extensions
sections.content:
Any extension that changes the grammar for the comparator or match-type will also affect how body works.

Wildcard matches used with body are exempt from the side effects of the variables extension in RFC 5229. They MUST NOT set match variables such as ${1} or ${2} from the text that matched a wildcard. If the variables extension is present, variable references inside the key strings or content type strings are still evaluated.
sections.eli5: If you add other Sieve tools to the box, the body test follows their rules for how words are compared. It just does not hand back the bits matched by wildcards.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Body matching can be expensive. The system MUST be sized and restricted so that even malicious use of body matching does not deny service to other users of the host system.

Filters that rely on string matches in the raw body of a message may be more general than intended. The RFC states plainly that text matches are no replacement for a spam, virus or other security related filtering system.
sections.eli5: Reading every letter takes effort, so the mailroom must not let one person's huge searches slow everyone else down. And a word search is not a guard against bad mail.

cells: The entire undecoded body as a single item, MIME boundaries and part headers included
Each MIME part whose content type is in the list, matched independently
Best-effort UTF-8 text extracted from the message
